source.title: A Practical Guide To Getting Started
source.author: Put This On

tips.text: Judge fit before brand or quality: ask whether a piece fits and flatters you before buying it.
tips.why: Fit is the biggest single improvement a beginner can make.

tips.text: Aim for a moderate fit, neither very slim nor very baggy.
tips.why: Both extremes are common mistakes; a middle fit is a safe baseline.

tips.text: Check that fabric hangs cleanly: pulling lines across chest or waist, or bunched folds, mean the fit is wrong.
tips.why: Tension and excess cloth are the clearest signs of poor fit.

tips.text: Don't size down to look slimmer.
tips.why: Tight clothes tend to make you look heavier, not thinner.

tips.text: Test fit while moving: a shirt shouldn't strain when you sit, and a jacket should let you lift your arms.
tips.why: Clothes have to work in motion, not just standing in a mirror.

tips.text: A jacket collar should rest against the back of your neck without a gap.
tips.why: A gaping collar is a basic sign of a poorly fitting jacket.

tips.text: Clear out clothes that are worn out, dated or never suited you, and sell or donate them.
tips.why: A smaller wardrobe of things you'll wear is easier to dress from.

tips.text: Alter pieces you like instead of replacing them: hem or taper trousers, shorten sleeves, take in shirts and jackets.
tips.why: Tailoring usually costs less than buying new.

tips.text: Buy jackets and shirts that fit the shoulders and chest, and trousers that fit the seat and thighs; most other things can be altered.
tips.why: Those areas are hard or impossible for a tailor to fix.

tips.text: Shop for the life you actually lead and what you wear most, not trends or a lifestyle you don't have.
tips.why: Clothes that suit your habits get worn; the rest sits unused.

tips.text: Start with plain basics: white tee, white and light blue shirts, blue jeans, grey wool trousers, khaki chinos, a dark suit, good boots.
tips.why: Simple pieces without logos or prints are a flexible foundation while your taste develops.

tips.text: Build a wardrobe of pieces that mix, not single outfits, in a narrow palette of blues, greys, browns, whites and tans.
tips.why: When colours coordinate, almost everything goes together.

tips.text: Buy fewer, better things, and avoid impulse purchases and fast fashion.
tips.why: Considered pieces stay satisfying for longer.

tips.text: While you're still learning, buy mid-priced pieces and treat early purchases as experiments.
tips.why: Your taste will change and you'll likely replace them.

tips.text: Spend most of your budget on outerwear and shoes, then knitwear.
tips.why: These pieces have the biggest impact on how you look.

tips.text: Look at second-hand and thrift shops, locally or online, for well-made clothes.
tips.why: Good pieces can be found for much less.

tips.text: Never buy something just because it's on sale.
tips.why: A discount doesn't make an unneeded or ill-fitting piece useful.

tips.text: Train your eye by studying outfits you admire: where seams fall, how cloth drapes and where garments end.
tips.why: Recognising good fit and proportion takes years of looking.

tips.text: Think about what an outfit says as a whole; changing one piece changes its message.
tips.why: Dressing works like writing: every element contributes.

tips.text: Have your feet measured properly before buying good shoes.
tips.why: Many men wear the wrong shoe size.

tips.text: Build your wardrobe slowly, drawing inspiration from film, art, music and subcultures and saving outfits you like.
tips.why: Taste develops gradually; rushing leads to regret buys.
